## Motivation {#motivation}

Training needs a rule for comparing predictions that make different kinds or sizes of mistakes.
A loss function measures how a prediction compares with its target.
The choice of loss determines which errors receive larger penalties and influences the predictions favoured by training.

## Loss, empirical risk, and the training objective {#loss-and-risk}

A loss function assigns a scalar penalty to a prediction–target pair:

$$
  \ell:\widehat{\mathcal Y}\times\mathcal Y\rightarrow\mathbb R.
$$

Here, $\widehat{\mathcal Y}$ is the set of allowed predictions and $\mathcal Y$ is the set of allowed targets.
For example, a regression loss can compare a real-valued prediction $\hat y$ with a real-valued target $y$.

Empirical risk is the average loss over a finite dataset of observed examples.
For $n\geq1$ examples $(x_i,y_i)$ and model predictions $\hat y_i=f_{\mathbf w}(x_i)$,

$$
  L(\mathbf w)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(f_{\mathbf w}(x_i),y_i).
$$

The inputs and targets are fixed; changing the [parameters]{.term key="parameter"} $\mathbf w$ changes the predictions and therefore the empirical risk.
A training objective is a scalar-valued function of the model parameters that training seeks to minimise.
It can be the empirical risk itself or include additional terms, such as a [regularisation penalty]{.term key="regularisation-penalty"}.
In this note, the objective is $L$.

A parameter value $\mathbf w^*$ is a global minimiser of $L$ if

$$
  L(\mathbf w^*)\leq L(\mathbf w)
  \quad\text{for every allowed }\mathbf w.
$$

## Comparing common losses {#comparison}

For a real-valued prediction and target, write the signed error as $e=\hat y-y$.

| Loss | Penalty for one example | Main feature |
|---|---|---|
| [Squared loss](#mse) | $e^2$ | The derivative grows in magnitude with the error. |
| [Absolute loss](#mae) | $\lvert e\rvert$ | The derivative has constant magnitude away from zero. |
| [Huber loss](#huber) | Quadratic near zero, linear beyond a threshold | The derivative is continuous and bounded. |
| [Cross-entropy](../mathematics/entropy.qmd#cross-entropy) | $-\ln p_y$ for an observed class $y$ | Penalises assigning low probability $p_y$ to the observed class. |

MSE and MAE are the averages of squared and absolute losses, respectively.
The distinction between an individual loss $\ell$ and its dataset average $L$ matters when interpreting formulas and gradients.

## Mean squared error {#mse}

Let $n\geq1$ be the number of examples, $y_i\in\mathbb R$ a target, and $\hat y_i\in\mathbb R$ its prediction.
Mean squared error (MSE) is the average squared loss:

$$
  L_{\mathrm{MSE}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat y_i-y_i)^2.
$$

For one shared real prediction $w$ and equally weighted targets, the unique MSE-minimising prediction is their arithmetic mean:

$$
  w^*=\bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i.
$$

This statement concerns a model that predicts the same adjustable number for every example.
A general model can make different predictions for different inputs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: why the mean minimises MSE"}

Suppose the model predicts $w$ for every example.
Then

$$
  L(w)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(w-y_i)^2.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $w$ gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  L'(w)
  &=\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(w-y_i)\\
  &=\frac2n\left(nw-\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i\right)\\
  &=2(w-\bar y).
  \end{aligned}
$$

The second line uses the fact that adding the same $w$ exactly $n$ times gives $nw$.
Setting $L'(w)=0$ gives $w=\bar y$.
Since $L''(w)=2>0$ everywhere, this stationary point is the unique global minimiser.

:::

## Squared error and the conditional mean {#conditional-mean}

Let $A$ be a random action chunk and $o$ the observed context.
Squared norms sum over the chunk's action coordinates.
Suppose the deployed model outputs one chunk $\hat A=f_\theta(o)$.
Under squared error, the unrestricted population-optimal point prediction is the conditional mean:

$$
  f^*(o)=\mathbb E[A\mid o].
$$

This statement assumes finite [second moments]{.term key="second-moment"} and optimisation over all measurable point predictors.
A finite neural network trained on finite data need not reach that ideal.
The sample-mean result above is the finite-data case when one number is shared across examples.

For an observation with equally likely scalar targets $-2$ and $+2$, this mean is $0$.
A small expected squared error does not establish that the resulting action is physically feasible.
For trajectories, the same issue can appear coordinate by coordinate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Proof: squared error selects the conditional mean"}

Fix the observation and write $\mu=\mathbb E[A\mid o]$.
For any proposed point prediction $b$,

$$
  b-A=(b-\mu)+(\mu-A).
$$

Expand the squared norm and take a conditional expectation:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb E[\|b-A\|^2\mid o]
  &=\|b-\mu\|^2\\
  &\quad+\mathbb E[\|A-\mu\|^2\mid o].
  \end{aligned}
$$

The cross term vanishes because $\mathbb E[\mu-A\mid o]=0$.
The second term does not depend on $b$, and the first is minimised at $b=\mu$.

:::

Giving a direct MSE regressor an independent random input does not by itself fix the objective.
If that input conveys no information about the training target, the conditional mean remains unchanged.
A generative construction needs an objective and conditioning scheme that give the random input a useful role.

## Mean absolute error {#mae}

Let $n\geq1$ be the number of examples, $y_i\in\mathbb R$ a target, and $\hat y_i\in\mathbb R$ its prediction.
Mean absolute error (MAE) is the average absolute difference between predictions and targets:

$$
  L_{\mathrm{MAE}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\hat y_i-y_i|.
$$

For one shared real prediction and equally weighted targets, MAE is minimised at a median.
For an odd number of observations, the minimiser is the middle observation after sorting them.
For an even number, every value between the two central sorted observations minimises MAE.
This differs from MSE because absolute distances change at a constant rate on either side of a target, whereas squared-error derivatives grow with error magnitude.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Proof: why a median minimises MAE"}

Sort the targets as $y_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq y_{(n)}$.
The factor $1/n$ does not change the minimisers, so consider the sum of absolute errors.
For any pair $a\leq b$, the triangle inequality gives

$$
  |w-a|+|w-b|\geq b-a,
$$

with equality exactly when $w\in[a,b]$.

If $n=2m$, pair the smallest target with the largest, the second smallest with the second largest, and so on.
Each pair attains its minimum when $w$ lies between its two targets.
The intersection of all these intervals is $[y_{(m)},y_{(m+1)}]$, so exactly those values minimise the total error.

If $n=2m+1$, the same pairing leaves the middle term $|w-y_{(m+1)}|$.
Choosing $w=y_{(m+1)}$ minimises every pair and makes that remaining term zero.
Every other choice makes the middle term positive without reducing any pair below its minimum, so this minimiser is unique.

:::

## Huber loss {#huber}

For signed error $e=\hat y-y$ and a fixed threshold $\delta>0$, Huber loss is

$$
  \ell_\delta(e)=
  \begin{cases}
  \frac12e^2,& |e|\leq\delta,\\[4pt]
  \delta\left(|e|-\frac12\delta\right),& |e|>\delta.
  \end{cases}
$$

The threshold $\delta$ determines where the penalty changes from quadratic to linear.
Its coefficients make the two branches meet with matching values and slopes.
The derivative is

$$
  \ell_\delta'(e)=
  \begin{cases}
  e,& |e|\leq\delta,\\
  \delta\,\operatorname{sign}(e),& |e|>\delta,
  \end{cases}
$$

where $\operatorname{sign}(e)$ is $+1$ for positive errors and $-1$ for negative errors.
The magnitude of the derivative is bounded by $\delta$.
For multiple examples, their Huber losses can be averaged to form an empirical risk.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: matching the two branches of Huber loss"}

On the positive side, the quadratic branch is $q(e)=\frac12e^2$.
At the threshold $e=\delta$, its value and slope are

$$
  q(\delta)=\frac12\delta^2,
  \qquad q'(\delta)=\delta.
$$

Suppose we extend it with a straight line $ae+b$.
Matching the slope requires $a=\delta$.
Matching the value then requires

$$
  \delta^2+b=\frac12\delta^2
  \quad\Rightarrow\quad
  b=-\frac12\delta^2.
$$

Thus, the positive linear branch must be $\delta e-\frac12\delta^2$.
Using $|e|$ extends this symmetrically to negative errors, giving

$$
  \delta\left(|e|-\frac12\delta\right).
$$

The subtraction term positions the linear branch so that it meets the quadratic branch exactly.
Differentiating the two branches gives the derivative above, with both formulas agreeing at $e=\pm\delta$.

:::

## Using the objective {#using-the-objective}

For the same two scalar errors $1$ and $3$, MSE is $(1+9)/2=5$ and MAE is $(1+3)/2=2$.
The larger error contributes nine times the smaller error's squared penalty, but only three times its absolute penalty.
This comparison concerns how each loss weights errors; the numerical values of two different losses are not themselves interchangeable quality scores.

MSE has squared target units, while MAE has the target's units.
The Huber threshold must be chosen relative to the scale of the error, so changing the coordinate normalization changes what a fixed threshold means.
Low training loss alone does not establish good deployment performance or physical feasibility.

[Gradient descent](../mathematics/optimization.qmd#gradient-descent) uses derivatives to update parameters.
[Subgradients](../mathematics/optimization.qmd#subgradients) describe supporting slopes for convex losses at corners.
A loss name alone does not identify which parameters receive its gradients; [knowledge insulation](../../literature-review/action/knowledge-insulation.qmd) makes this distinction explicit.

## Connections and boundaries {#connections}

[Cross-entropy](../mathematics/entropy.qmd#cross-entropy) penalises predicted class probabilities, while [zero-one loss](../mathematics/entropy.qmd#zero-one-loss) counts incorrect class predictions.
[The ELBO](../mathematics/elbo.qmd) combines reconstruction likelihood and a latent-distribution penalty.
[Diffusion Policy](../../literature-review/action/diffusion-policy.qmd) uses squared error to predict noise, so its conditioning and target differ from direct action regression.
[Generative action models](generative-models.qmd#questions) compares objectives for actions, noise, and velocity.
